passage.text: When the students in our town started a school libraries project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving reading corners. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

passage.text: My passion for international cooking began when I tried a Korean dish at a friend's house last year. (16) ..... The flavours were completely different from anything I had tasted before, and I wanted to learn how to make similar dishes at home. I started following several food bloggers who specialised in Asian cuisine, and I learned about ingredients I had never heard of before, such as gochujang and miso paste.

I started by watching online videos and following recipes from different countries around the world. (17) ..... My first attempts were disasters — I burned the rice and added way too much chilli, making the food almost impossible to eat. I learned to appreciate that failure is part of the learning process, and each burnt dish taught me something important about cooking times and temperature control.

My grandmother, who was an experienced cook, offered to guide me through some basic cooking techniques. (18) ..... She taught me how to balance flavours properly and adjust seasoning gradually until the dish tasted just right. She showed me how to prepare ingredients before starting to cook and explained why certain flavour combinations work better together than others in different types of dishes.

After several months of regular practice, I invited my family to try a three-course meal I had prepared. (19) ..... They were surprised by how authentic the dishes tasted and encouraged me to keep experimenting with new recipes. My father, who is usually not very adventurous with food, asked for seconds of the main course, which was the highest compliment I could have received from him that evening.

Cooking has become much more than a hobby for me — it is a way to connect with other cultures. (20) ..... I now keep a journal of recipes from every country I learn about, and I hope to taste authentic food one day. I have started a small blog where I share my cooking experiences and the recipes I have learned from different countries around the world.
